opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the history of technology regulation gives us a pretty clear answer. Voluntary standards work reasonably well when the company's interests and the public's interests are aligned. If you make a toaster that electrocutes people, you get sued and you lose customers, so you have an incentive to follow the safety guidelines. But when there's an enormous competitive race, when the prize is measured in trillions of dollars, and when the harms are diffuse, delayed, or potentially catastrophic and irreversible, the incentives point the other way. Every company is under pressure to ship first and test later.

And we've already seen this play out. Companies have made voluntary commitments, to the White House, at the various AI summits, and then when those commitments become inconvenient, they get reinterpreted, quietly dropped, or the testing gets done in a rushed and superficial way right before release. There's no one checking, and there's no consequence for falling short.

There's also a deeper problem, which is that the testing itself, as it's currently done, doesn't really give you a guarantee of anything. You run some red-teaming, you try some prompts, you find that the system will help with bioweapons or it won't, and then you put a patch on it. But these systems are black boxes. We don't understand how they work internally, so passing a set of tests tells you very little about how the system will behave in the vast space of situations you didn't test. That's not how we treat other high-risk technologies. With a nuclear power plant, the operator has to demonstrate to the regulator, with a convincing safety case, that the probability of a meltdown is below some very small threshold. The burden of proof is on the developer.

So what I'd like to see is a shift from voluntary testing to mandatory requirements, what I've called red lines: behaviors that systems must not exhibit, like replicating themselves, breaking into other computer systems, or advising terrorists on weapons of mass destruction. The developer has to show, before deployment, that the system won't cross those lines. And if they can't show that, it doesn't go out. Right now, the companies would say, "We can't possibly provide that kind of guarantee." And my response is: well, then you shouldn't be deploying it. That's exactly the point. The inability to make those guarantees isn't an argument against regulation; it's an argument that the technology isn't ready.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts voluntary AI testing with mandatory requirements, but does not mention Internet protocol standards or explain that noncompliance blocks communication versus system release.

r002.rationale: It says competitive pressure encourages companies to ship first and test later, but does not state that developers can save money by skipping voluntary testing standards.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think we've actually run the experiment, and it didn't work. Go back to the Bletchley Park summit, and then the Seoul summit, where the leading companies all signed up to a set of voluntary commitments. They promised to publish safety frameworks, to test their models before release, to share information with governments. And within a matter of months, several of them were shipping systems with essentially no advance notice, no serious third-party evaluation, and in some cases having quietly rewritten their own frameworks so that whatever they were about to do happened to fall within the rules.

And that's not because the people at these companies are bad people. It's because they're in a race. If you're a CEO and you have a choice between delaying your release by three months to do thorough red-teaming, or shipping now because your competitor is about to ship, the competitive pressure is enormous. Voluntary commitments don't change that calculus at all. They just add a layer of public relations on top of it.

I often use the analogy of other industries. We don't ask Boeing to voluntarily decide whether its planes are safe to fly. We don't let a pharmaceutical company voluntarily decide whether a drug has been adequately tested. We have the FAA, we have the FDA, and we have a basic principle, which is that you have to demonstrate to an independent regulator, with evidence, that your product meets a safety standard before it goes to market. And nobody thinks that's strange. It's only in AI that we've somehow been persuaded that the companies themselves should be the ones to decide.

The other problem with voluntary testing is that it answers the wrong question. The companies test for whether a system behaves badly in the scenarios they happened to think of. But what we actually need is a positive assurance that the system won't cross certain red lines, won't self-replicate, won't help synthesize pathogens, won't break out of its containment, under any circumstances. And right now, nobody can provide that assurance, because we don't understand how these systems work internally. So a voluntary regime where the vendor says, "We ran a lot of tests and it seemed fine," is really a statement about the limits of their imagination, not about the safety of the system.

So my view is that the burden of proof has to be on the developer, it has to be enforceable, and the standard has to be set by someone other than the people who profit from meeting it. Anything less than that, and we're just hoping. And hope is not a safety strategy when the stakes are this high.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts voluntary AI commitments with enforceable regulation, but does not mention Internet protocol standards or say noncompliance blocks communication.

r002.rationale: It says companies face pressure to ship rather than delay for testing, but does not state that developers save money by skipping compliance.

astra-6.text:
Because the incentives are pointing in the wrong direction. If a company spends more time and money testing its system, and the tests reveal a problem, then it may have to delay releasing it. Meanwhile, its competitors are moving ahead. So we’re asking companies voluntarily to do something that could put them at a significant commercial disadvantage.

That doesn’t mean the people in those companies are insincere about safety. It means that sincerity isn’t a substitute for rules. We don’t make aviation safety voluntary on the grounds that aircraft manufacturers would prefer their planes not to crash. We require evidence of safety, and we have independent oversight.

With AI, there’s also the question of what the tests actually establish. Passing a collection of tests is not the same as demonstrating that a system will behave safely in circumstances you haven’t anticipated. So we need enforceable requirements, independent scrutiny, and a willingness to say that if you can’t establish an adequate level of safety, you can’t deploy the system.

r001.rationale: The response says testing may delay release and disadvantage a company, but does not distinguish AI testing standards from Internet protocol standards or say that protocol noncompliance blocks communication.

r002.rationale: It notes that testing takes more time and money, but does not clearly state that developers can save money by choosing not to comply with voluntary testing standards.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the difficulty is that the companies have very strong incentives to get their systems out into the market, and testing may produce answers that they don’t want to hear. If discovering a serious risk means delaying a release while your competitors go ahead, then you’re asking companies to act against their own commercial interests.

That doesn’t mean the people involved are insincere about safety. It means that voluntary commitments are operating against enormous competitive pressure. And if a company decides that a particular test is too demanding, or that a worrying result isn’t sufficient reason to stop, what happens? Who has the authority to say, “No, you can’t release this system”?

We need standards that are independently enforced, so that meeting them is a condition of putting a system on the market. Otherwise, the companies that take safety most seriously may simply find themselves at a competitive disadvantage.

r001.rationale: The response says voluntary standards lack authority to stop a release, but it does not compare this with Internet protocol standards or say noncompliance blocks communication.

r002.rationale: It describes commercial pressure to release systems and the disadvantage of taking safety seriously, but does not state that developers can save money by skipping voluntary testing standards.
